title: Alice Kyteler Trial: First Combined Heresy-Witchcraft Prosecution in Ireland
description: Alice Kyteler of Kilkenny was accused in 1324 by Richard de Ledrede, Bishop of Ossory, of leading a sect that denied Christ, sacrificed animals at crossroads to a demon called Robin Son of Art, and prepared magical powders from the flesh of dead men mixed with worms and herbs. Kyteler herself escaped to England, but her servant Petronilla de Meath was flogged and burned — the first person executed for witchcraft in Ireland. The Kyteler case is notable for combining standard sorcery accusations (maleficium, poisoning) with specifically heretical elements (diabolical pact, renunciation of Christ) in a single indictment, representing an early example of the converging legal and theological frameworks that would become standard in later prosecutions.
historiographical_note: The Kyteler case has attracted attention as an unusually early example of fully developed witch accusations against an elite woman. Historians including L.S. Davidson and J.O. Ward (who edited the primary source) have noted its combination of continental demonological elements with local Irish concerns, suggesting the importation of new frameworks by a bishop trained in continental theology.
source_method: Contemporary account by Richard de Ledrede; Davidson and Ward edition of the trial record; secondary scholarship
